content:
The creator of Netflix’s “Black Doves” took on a fan over their complaints about a “This gun kills fascists” sticker on a new character’s weapon.

The response arrived after X user @ChatsWithEm weighed in on a shot from the spy action thriller showing Laila Joshi (an agent for the “Black Doves” spy-for-hire organization played by Ambika Mod) carrying a gun with the anti-fascist sticker in the Season 2 finale.

“Oh dear Netflix. . Oh dear 🤬 I was LOVING the series Black Doves. Until I saw this,” the user wrote of the spy show starring Keira Knightley and Ben Whishaw.

“I find this HIGHLY irresponsible glorifying gun crime and with stickers on of who the depicted gun targets. Knowing there are many who describe anyone as facists these days from the conservative , elderly , those who want Peace in Russia , to those who support Israelis from persecution or those who think pronouns aren’t labels to play with,” the post read.

“And after the death of Charlie Kirk .. I find this deeply concerning and inflammatory. You should be bringing people together not hardening the divide,” it continued.

Screenwriter Joe Barton kept it short and sweet, responding to the user, “Sounds as if you just like fascists tbh.”

Barton, minutes after the user criticized him for having “not a very professional response,” hit back, “Apologies. In my professional opinion it sounds as if you just like fascists tbh.”

The sticker appears to be a spin on “This machine kills fascists,” a slogan that appeared on the guitars of American folk icon Woody Guthrie signaling his view on creating music as an act of resistance against fascism in World War II and beyond.

The musician borrowed the slogan, which was being stamped on war machinery at the time, per Deana McCloud, executive director and chief curator of the Woody Guthrie Center, speaking in an interview with the “Road to Now” podcast.

“And he saw it, and his thinking was, ‘Well, my instruments are my machine. My instruments are the way that I fight against fascism,’” she said.

Guthrie — when questioned by Pete Seeger why he was still putting the slogan on his guitar after Adolf Hitler’s death — stressed that as long as there are people trying to “keep the common man down, the fascists are still here,” McCloud said.

The slogan has inspired the likes of Julien Baker and Rage Against The Machine’s Tom Morello to put their own messages on their guitars.

And Jack White made a nod to the slogan when he sued President Donald Trump — then a GOP presidential nominee — in 2024 over his campaign’s use of The White Stripes’ “Seven Nation Army,” writing on social media, “This machine sues fascists.”
